plan: [ This auction is strategically equivalent to a second‑price (Vickrey) auction: highest sealed bid wins and pays the second-highest bid. In such auctions, bidding one’s true private value is a weakly dominant strategy that maximizes expected profit. Overbidding risks negative surplus if I win above value; underbidding risks losing profitable wins. There’s only 1 round, so no dynamic considerations or learning. My value is $28, so I will set my exit (sealed) bid equal to 28 to ensure I win whenever the price is below my value and never pay above it. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction: the winner pays the second-highest sealed bid. With independent private values and risk-neutrality, bidding my true value is a (weakly) dominant strategy. Overbidding risks paying more than my value if others also bid high; underbidding risks losing when the price would have been below my value. There’s no prior history to exploit and only one round, so no learning or signaling value. Therefore, I bid my exact value of 23 to maximize expected profit. ]

[ This is strategically equivalent to a second-price auction (winner pays the second-highest sealed bid). The weakly dominant strategy is to bid my true value to maximize expected profit regardless of others’ behavior. Overbidding risks negative surplus if the second price exceeds my value; underbidding risks losing when winning would be profitable. No prior history to exploit this round. Therefore, I will bid exactly my value, $36. If there's a tie at 36, the winner is chosen randomly, which is acceptable given zero-profit at that price. ]
